hints: Look at the state symbols in reaction 1 and identify which products would be seen leaving the solid and liquid mixture.
walkthrough:
Read what you can actually see**
Picture the reaction vessel. You start with a solid $\text{BaCl}_2\cdot 2\text{H}_2\text{O(s)}$ and a liquid $\text{SOCl}_2\text{(l)}$. The products include a solid $\text{BaCl}_2\text{(s)}$ plus two gases, $\text{SO}_2\text{(g)}$ and $\text{HCl(g)}$.

Link HCl gas to a classic observation**
$\text{HCl(g)}$ is famous for forming white steamy fumes in moist air because it dissolves in water vapour to give tiny droplets of hydrochloric acid. That is the one clear visible change as effervescence occurs.
Final answer: White steamy fumes observed (due to $\text{HCl(g)}$).

hints: Recall that entropy is a measure of disorder, but Cambridge wants disorder of both particles and energy quanta, not just particles.
walkthrough:
Go beyond just disorder**
Many students say disorder only. At A Level, think of two types of spreading: particles can spread out in space in more ways, and energy can be shared among more energy levels in more ways. Entropy counts both.

Give the precise definition**
So entropy measures the number of possible arrangements of particles and energy in a system. More arrangements means higher entropy, for example gas has much higher entropy than solid.
Final answer: Entropy, $S$, is a measure of the number of possible arrangements of particles and energy in a system.

hints: Compare the total moles of gas on each side of reaction 1 and recall which state has by far the largest entropy.
walkthrough:
Count the gas moles**
Reactants are $\text{BaCl}_2\cdot 2\text{H}_2\text{O(s)} + 2\text{SOCl}_2\text{(l)}$, so zero moles of gas. Products are $\text{BaCl}_2\text{(s)} + 2\text{SO}_2\text{(g)} + 4\text{HCl(g)}$, so six moles of gas.

Connect gas to entropy**
Gases have hugely more ways to arrange particles and energy than solids and liquids. Creating six moles of gas gives a very large increase in disorder, so $\Delta S^\ominus$ is large and positive.
Final answer: Large increase in moles of gas from reactants to products, six moles of gas are formed from solid and liquid, so much more disorder.

hints: Start with $\Delta H_r^\ominus = \sum \Delta H_f^\ominus(\text{products}) - \sum \Delta H_f^\ominus(\text{reactants})$, remembering to multiply each value by its stoichiometric coefficient.
Recall $\Delta G^\ominus = \Delta H^\ominus - T\Delta S^\ominus$ and convert temperature to kelvin and entropy to $\text{kJ K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$ so units match.
Substitute $T = 298\text{ K}$, $\Delta H^\ominus$ in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ and $\Delta S^\ominus = 0.768\text{ kJ K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$ to find $\Delta G^\ominus$.
walkthrough:
Calculate enthalpy change from formation data**
Use Hess cycle thinking: formation enthalpies already include elements to compounds, so:
$$\Delta H_r^\ominus = \sum \Delta H_f^\ominus(\text{products}) - \sum \Delta H_f^\ominus(\text{reactants})$$
$$\Delta H_r^\ominus = [(-859) + 2(-297) + 4(-92)] - [(-1460) + 2(-246)]$$
$$\Delta H_r^\ominus = (-859 -594 -368) - (-1460 -492) = -1821 + 1952 = +131\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$ The reaction is endothermic.

Set up Gibbs free energy correctly**
Feasibility depends on both enthalpy and entropy:
$$\Delta G^\ominus = \Delta H^\ominus - T\Delta S^\ominus$$
Temperature must be in kelvin: $T = 25 + 273 = 298\text{ K}$. Entropy must be in $\text{kJ}$, so $+768\text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1} = 0.768\text{ kJ K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$. This unit match is the most common slip.

Substitute and evaluate**
$$\Delta G^\ominus = 131 - (298 \times 0.768)$$
$$\Delta G^\ominus = 131 - 228.9 = -97.9\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$
Negative $\Delta G^\ominus$ means the reaction is feasible at $25^{\circ}\text{C}$, driven by the large positive entropy change despite being endothermic.

Final answer: $\Delta H_r^\ominus = +131\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$
$\Delta G^\ominus = \Delta H^\ominus - T\Delta S^\ominus = 131 - (298 \times 0.768) = -97.9\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$

hints: Identify spectator ions $\text{Na}^+$ and $\text{Cl}^-$ that stay in solution, and focus on $\text{Ba}^{2+}$, $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$ and water forming $\text{BaCrO}_4$ and $\text{H}^+$.
walkthrough:
Cancel what does not change**
Mixing $\text{BaCl}_2$ and $\text{Na}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ brings $\text{Ba}^{2+}$, $\text{Cl}^-$, $\text{Na}^+$ and $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$ together. $\text{Na}^+$ and $\text{Cl}^-$ remain in solution unchanged, so omit them.

Balance the chromate conversion**
Dichromate plus water gives chromate precipitate plus acid:
$$2\text{Ba}^{2+}(\text{aq}) + \text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}(\text{aq}) + \text{H}_2\text{O(l)} \rightarrow 2\text{BaCrO}_4(\text{s}) + 2\text{H}^{+}(\text{aq})$$
Check atoms and charge: $2\text{ Ba}$, $2\text{ Cr}$, $8\text{ O}$, $2\text{ H}$ and $+2$ charge on each side. The $\text{H}^+$ explains why an acidic solution remains.

hints: Recall what happens to the energies of d orbitals when ligands approach a transition metal ion.
Think about what happens when an electron absorbs a photon of exactly the right energy in the visible region.
Relate the colour absorbed to the colour seen, remembering the seen colour is what is not absorbed.
walkthrough:
Picture the d orbitals splitting**
In the free ion the five d orbitals have the same energy. When ligands approach, they repel d electrons unequally, so the d set splits into lower and higher energy groups with a d-d energy gap that matches visible light energies.

Promote an electron with light**
An electron in a lower d orbital can absorb a photon, $h\nu$, of exactly that gap energy and jump to a higher d orbital. This is d electron excitation.

Explain the observed yellow**
Only certain wavelengths or frequencies are absorbed. The remaining wavelengths are transmitted or reflected. What you see is the complementary colour to what was absorbed, in this case yellow for $\text{BaCrO}_4\text{(s)}$.

Final answer: d orbitals split into two sets of different energies.
Electron is promoted from lower to higher d orbital by absorbing visible light.
Colour seen is complementary to colour absorbed, transmitted light is seen.

hints: Recall $\Delta H_{sol} = -\Delta H_{latt} + \Delta H_{hyd}$ in magnitude terms, and consider how cation size affects both terms down Group 2.
Compare how quickly lattice enthalpy and hydration enthalpy change when the cation gets larger but the sulfate anion is large and almost constant in size.
Link the resulting trend in $\Delta H_{sol}$ to solubility, remembering more endothermic solution means less soluble.
walkthrough:
Track both enthalpies down the group**
Going from $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ to $\text{Ba}^{2+}$, ionic radius increases and charge density falls. Both the lattice enthalpy of $\text{MSO}_4$ and the hydration enthalpy of $\text{M}^{2+}$ become less exothermic or less negative because attraction to anions and to water weakens.

Decide which changes faster**
The sulfate ion $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ is large, so changing the cation size has only a small effect on lattice energy. Hydration involves the small water molecule packing closely around the cation, so $\Delta H_{hyd}^\ominus$ falls much more steeply. Hydration dominates the trend.

Combine to get solubility trend**
Since:
$$\Delta H_{sol}^\ominus = -\Delta H_{latt}^\ominus + \Delta H_{hyd}^\ominus$$
the faster fall in hydration makes $\Delta H_{sol}^\ominus$ become less exothermic and then more endothermic down the group. Dissolving becomes less favourable, so solubility decreases and $\text{BaSO}_4$ is least soluble.

Final answer: Both $\Delta H_{latt}^\ominus$ and $\Delta H_{hyd}^\ominus$ become less exothermic down the group.
$\Delta H_{hyd}^\ominus$ decreases by more, it is the dominant factor.
$\Delta H_{sol}^\ominus$ becomes less exothermic or more endothermic, so solubility decreases.
